triage.name: Ear Infections
triage.reason: Otitis media is a very common pediatric diagnosis with a classic presentation reachable by history and otoscopic exam.

exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: Most common in children under 3 years; about three of four children have at least one episode by age 3
More frequent in boys than girls in early childhood
Less common in adults, in whom it often follows an upper respiratory infection or occurs with a chronic eardrum problem

risk_factors.text: Recent upper respiratory infection or cold
Family history of frequent ear infections

family_history: Frequent ear infections in a parent or sibling
Ear tubes placed in a sibling
exposures: Recent cold or flu-like illness in the household

chief_complaints.text: He keeps pulling at his ear and crying
She has a fever and won't stop fussing
There's fluid coming out of his ear
He can't hear me well since his cold

hpi.onset: Usually develops over 1–2 days, often during or shortly after a cold
hpi.duration: Symptoms typically present within the first few days of illness
hpi.progression: Ear pain builds over hours to a day, is worst at night, and may ease if the eardrum ruptures and drains
hpi.location: One or both ears; deep inside the ear
hpi.radiation: May spread to the jaw or side of the head on the affected side
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; young children show it as intense crying and poor sleep
hpi.timing: Constant, often worse at night and when lying down

associated_symptoms.text: Irritability or fussiness in young children
Pulling or tugging at the ear
Recent or current runny nose and cough
Trouble hearing or seeming not to respond to sound

pertinent_negatives: Swelling, redness, or pain when pulling on the outer ear
Pain with chewing or opening the mouth
Swelling or redness behind the ear pushing it forward

negatives: Pain when moving the outer ear
Swelling or redness behind the ear
Redness or swelling behind the ear

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants cannot localize pain; they present with inconsolable crying, poor feeding, fever, and ear tugging rather than saying their ear hurts.
Adults often have less fever and more hearing loss or ear fullness, and the episode may follow a cold or be associated with chronic eardrum disease.
Can progress rapidly with severe pain, high fever, and risk of complications such as mastoiditis or intracranial spread.

general.mild: Alert, playful between bouts of discomfort; may tug at the affected ear
general.moderate: Fussy and irritable, consolable by a parent, prefers to be held upright
general.severe: Ill-appearing, continuously crying, difficult to console, poor feeding
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, lethargic or inconsolable, with signs of a complication such as mastoid swelling or meningismus

findings.maneuver: Insert the otoscope and inspect the tympanic membrane, comparing both ears
findings.finding: Bulging, opacified tympanic membrane with loss of the normal light reflex

findings.maneuver: Inspect the tympanic membrane color and vascularity
Use pneumatic otoscopy to gently puff air against the tympanic membrane
findings.finding: Decreased or absent mobility of the tympanic membrane

findings.maneuver: Inspect for fluid behind the tympanic membrane
findings.finding: Air-fluid level or bubbles behind the tympanic membrane

findings.maneuver: Inspect the external canal and tympanic membrane for drainage
findings.finding: Purulent drainage in the canal from a perforated tympanic membrane
Canal is patent and not swollen or tender, with no debris or discharge

findings.maneuver: Gently pull the auricle and press on the tragus
findings.finding: No pain with manipulation of the outer ear

findings.maneuver: Palpate behind the ear over the mastoid bone
findings.finding: No tenderness, swelling, or redness behind the ear

findings.maneuver: Compare the position of both auricles from above and behind the patient
findings.finding: Auricle is in normal position, not pushed forward or outward

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oropharynx and nasal passages
findings.finding: Erythematous pharynx or purulent nasal discharge from a concurrent upper respiratory infection

findings.maneuver: Palpate the anterior and posterior cervical lymph node chains
Flex the neck and assess for resistance
Assess mental status, cranial nerves, and gait if the child is ambulatory
findings.finding: Alert and age-appropriate, no focal deficits or ataxia
Clear breath sounds without crackles or wheezing

imaging.preferred_when: Every patient with suspected acute otitis media; the primary diagnostic study

findings.text: Bulging, opacified tympanic membrane with loss of the light reflex
Reduced or absent tympanic membrane mobility with insufflation
Air-fluid level or bubbles behind the tympanic membrane
Purulent drainage in the canal from a perforated tympanic membrane

imaging.preferred_when: When the tympanic membrane cannot be well seen or the diagnosis is uncertain; also used to follow effusion

findings.text: Flat (type B) tympanogram indicating middle ear effusion
Reduced peak compliance with negative middle ear pressure

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected mastoiditis, intracranial extension, or other complication

findings.text: Opacification of the middle ear and mastoid air cells
Coalescent mastoiditis with loss of mastoid trabeculae
Subperiosteal abscess or epidural or intracranial collection

imaging.study: MRI brain and temporal bones with and without IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected intracranial complication such as meningitis, epidural abscess, or sigmoid sinus thrombosis

findings.text: Meningeal enhancement or extra-axial fluid collection
Sigmoid sinus filling defect suggesting thrombosis
Clouding of mastoid air cells; low sensitivity and rarely used

initial.why: Confirms middle ear effusion and inflammation; the diagnostic standard for acute otitis media

confirmatory.why: Documents middle ear effusion when otoscopy is equivocal or the canal is obscured
confirmatory.only_if: otoscopy is nondiagnostic or the tympanic membrane cannot be clearly seen

supporting.why: Not routine; may show leukocytosis in severe or complicated disease
supporting.only_if: severe illness, toxic appearance, or concern for a complication

supporting.why: Not routine; may support a bacterial process in severe or complicated disease
supporting.only_if: severe illness or concern for a complication

supporting.why: Evaluates for mastoiditis or intracranial extension
supporting.only_if: swelling or redness behind the ear, auricle pushed forward, or persistent high fever despite treatment

supporting.test: MRI brain and temporal bones with and without IV contrast
supporting.only_if: meningismus, focal neurologic findings, seizures, or suspected sinus thrombosis

not_indicated.why: No established role in acute otitis media
Reserved for toxic-appearing or septic patients; not part of routine workup
Only if meningitis is suspected; not part of otitis media workup
Low sensitivity and superseded by CT when a complication is suspected

decision_points: Diagnose acute otitis media when there is moderate to severe bulging of the tympanic membrane, or new-onset ear drainage not explained by otitis externa, or mild bulging with recent ear pain or marked erythema
Distinguish acute otitis media from otitis media with effusion, which has fluid without acute inflammation and does not need antibiotics
Consider watchful waiting without antibiotics for 48 to 72 hours in children 6 to 23 months with nonsevere illness and in children 2 years and older with mild symptoms, when follow-up is reliable

Treat with antibiotics when the child is under 6 months, has severe symptoms such as moderate or severe pain, fever of 39 degrees C or higher, or otorrhea, or when symptoms have not improved in 48 to 72 hours
Refer for tympanostomy tubes when there are recurrent episodes or persistent effusion with hearing loss
Image when there is mastoid swelling, auricle displacement, meningismus, or failure to improve on appropriate antibiotics

criteria.name: Acute otitis media diagnostic criteria
criteria.summary: Requires a history of acute onset plus findings of middle ear effusion and signs of middle ear inflammation on otoscopy.
items: Acute onset of signs and symptoms such as ear pain, ear tugging, or fever
Middle ear effusion shown by bulging tympanic membrane, decreased mobility, or otorrhea
Middle ear inflammation shown by distinct erythema or ear pain

criteria.name: American Academy of Pediatrics antibiotic decision framework
criteria.summary: Antibiotic treatment is recommended based on age and severity, with observation offered in selected low-risk children.
items: Age under 6 months: antibiotics for all
Age 6 to 23 months: antibiotics for severe illness; observation option for nonsevere illness with reliable follow-up
Age 2 years and older: antibiotics for severe illness; observation option for mild illness

differential.name: Otitis media with effusion
differential.why_considered: Fluid behind the eardrum is common after a cold and can cause ear fullness and mild hearing loss, but it lacks acute inflammation.

history: No significant ear pain or fever
Hearing muffled or feeling of fullness, often noticed after a cold
Symptoms may persist for weeks without worsening
exam: Retracted or neutral tympanic membrane with visible fluid level or bubbles, but not bulging
Reduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy without marked erythema
imaging: Flat (type B) tympanogram indicating effusion without acute inflammation

differential.name: Otitis externa
differential.why_considered: Ear pain is the cardinal symptom, and the external canal can look red and swollen.

history: Pain worse when pulling on the ear or chewing
Itching or discharge from the canal
exam: Tenderness with manipulation of the auricle or tragus
Swollen, erythematous external canal with debris or discharge
Tympanic membrane may be normal or obscured but not bulging

differential.name: Mastoiditis
differential.why_considered: It is a complication of acute otitis media and can present with persistent ear pain and fever.
differential.trigger: Swelling, redness, or tenderness behind the ear, or the auricle pushed forward

history: Ear pain and fever that persist or worsen despite appropriate antibiotic treatment
exam: Swelling, erythema, and tenderness over the mastoid bone
labs: Leukocytosis and elevated inflammatory markers may be present
imaging: CT temporal bone showing opacification of mastoid air cells, loss of trabeculae, or subperiosteal abscess

differential.name: Meningitis
differential.why_considered: Fever and irritability in a young child can be caused by meningitis, and it can complicate or mimic ear infection.
differential.trigger: Severe headache, stiff neck, photophobia, lethargy, or a toxic appearance

history: Severe headache, neck stiffness, vomiting, confusion, or lethargy
exam: Nuchal rigidity, positive Brudzinski or Kernig sign
May have a bulging fontanelle in infants
labs: CSF analysis showing pleocytosis, elevated protein, and low glucose
imaging: MRI with meningeal enhancement; CT may be normal early

differential.name: Referred otalgia from dental or pharyngeal source
differential.why_considered: Pain can be referred to the ear from the teeth, jaw, or throat without middle ear disease.

history: Pain with chewing or opening the mouth
exam: Normal tympanic membrane without effusion or bulging
Dental caries, gingival tenderness, or pharyngeal erythema

severity.mild: Ear pain is mild and brief, fever is low-grade or absent, the child is playful between discomfort, and otoscopy shows mild bulging with erythema.
severity.moderate: Ear pain is moderate to severe, fever is present, the child is fussy but consolable, and otoscopy shows distinct bulging with opacification and reduced mobility.
severity.severe: High fever, severe pain, poor feeding, ill appearance, and otoscopy shows marked bulging or spontaneous perforation with otorrhea.
severity.critical: Toxic appearance with signs of a complication such as mastoid swelling, meningismus, focal neurologic deficits, or hemodynamic instability.

red_flags.finding: Swelling, redness, or tenderness behind the ear, or the auricle pushed forward
red_flags.meaning: Mastoiditis; requires urgent imaging and IV antibiotics, often surgical drainage

red_flags.finding: Severe headache, stiff neck, photophobia, or altered mental status
red_flags.meaning: Possible meningitis or intracranial extension; needs urgent lumbar puncture and imaging

red_flags.finding: Fever of 39°C (102.2°F) or higher with toxic appearance
red_flags.meaning: Severe infection or complication; consider blood cultures and broader workup
Facial nerve involvement from middle ear inflammation or complication

red_flags.finding: Persistent high fever and ear pain despite 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotics
red_flags.meaning: Treatment failure or complication; reassess and consider imaging

complications.name: Tympanic membrane perforation with otorrhea
clues: Sudden relief of pain followed by drainage from the ear

complications.name: Mastoiditis
clues: Swelling, redness, and tenderness behind the ear

complications.name: Intracranial complications (meningitis, epidural abscess, sigmoid sinus thrombosis)
clues: Persistent high fever and toxic appearance

complications.name: Chronic suppurative otitis media
clues: Ear drainage lasting more than 6 weeks

complications.name: Hearing loss from persistent middle ear effusion
clues: Muffled hearing or delayed speech in children
Fluid behind the eardrum persisting for weeks after the acute infection

special_populations.differences: Cannot localize pain; present with inconsolable crying, poor feeding, fever, and ear tugging. Diagnosis relies on otoscopy. Antibiotics are recommended for all infants under 6 months.
Most common in children under 3 years. Watchful waiting may be appropriate for selected children 6 months and older with nonsevere illness and reliable follow-up.
Less common; often follows an upper respiratory infection or occurs with chronic eardrum disease. May have less fever and more hearing loss or ear fullness.
Can progress rapidly with severe pain, high fever, and increased risk of mastoiditis or intracranial spread. Lower threshold for antibiotics and imaging.

key_questions.question: When did the ear pain or fussiness start, and how has it changed since then?
key_questions.looking_for: Acute onset over 1–2 days, often during or just after a cold; pain building and worst at night

key_questions.question: Which ear is bothering him, and does he seem to hear less well on that side?
key_questions.looking_for: One or both ears, deep inside; muffled hearing or not responding to sound

key_questions.question: Has there been any fluid or pus draining from the ear?
key_questions.looking_for: New otorrhea not explained by otitis externa; drainage often follows sudden relief of pain

key_questions.question: Has he had a cold, runny nose, or cough recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent or current upper respiratory infection, which commonly precedes acute otitis media

key_questions.question: Any fever, and if so how high has it been measured?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever, especially 39°C (102.2°F) or higher, which pushes toward antibiotic treatment

key_questions.question: How is he sleeping and eating?
key_questions.looking_for: Trouble sleeping, decreased appetite, poor feeding in an infant

key_questions.question: Does he tug or pull at the ear, or cry more than usual?
key_questions.looking_for: Ear tugging and irritability, the main way young children show ear pain

key_questions.question: Does anything make the pain better or worse — lying flat, swallowing, chewing, pulling on the ear?
key_questions.looking_for: Worse lying flat and with swallowing or chewing; pain with pulling on the outer ear suggests otitis externa instead

key_questions.question: Has he had ear infections before, and have ear tubes ever been placed?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent episodes or prior tympanostomy tubes, which change management

key_questions.question: Does he have any condition that affects the ears or immune system, such as Down syndrome, cleft palate, or an immunodeficiency?
key_questions.looking_for: Comorbidities that raise the risk of persistent or complicated disease

key_questions.question: Does anyone in the home smoke, and does he attend daycare or preschool?
key_questions.looking_for: Secondhand smoke exposure and group childcare, both strong risk factors

key_questions.question: How is he fed — breast, bottle, and does he lie flat with the bottle?
key_questions.looking_for: Bottle feeding while lying flat; not being breastfed

key_questions.question: Does anyone in the family get frequent ear infections or need ear tubes?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of frequent ear infections or tympanostomy tubes

key_questions.question: Has he had any swelling, redness, or pain behind the ear, or does the ear look pushed forward?
key_questions.looking_for: Mastoiditis — needs urgent imaging and IV antibiotics

key_questions.question: Any severe headache, stiff neck, confusion, or unusual sleepiness?
key_questions.looking_for: Meningitis or intracranial extension — urgent workup

key_questions.question: Any weakness or drooping on one side of the face?
key_questions.looking_for: Facial nerve involvement from middle ear inflammation or a complication

key_questions.question: Has he been swimming or getting water in his ears?
key_questions.looking_for: Water exposure, which points toward otitis externa rather than otitis media

key_questions.question: Any vomiting, diarrhea, or abdominal pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Vomiting sometimes occurs; diarrhea and abdominal pain are not typical and suggest another cause

reasoning_points: Acute onset of ear pain, ear tugging, or fever, usually during or shortly after a cold
Middle ear effusion shown by a bulging tympanic membrane, decreased mobility on pneumatic otoscopy, or new otorrhea
Middle ear inflammation shown by distinct erythema or ear pain
Otitis media with effusion considered and distinguished — fluid without acute inflammation does not need antibiotics
Otitis externa considered and distinguished — pain with pulling on the auricle or tragus and a swollen canal point away from otitis media
Age and severity used to decide between immediate antibiotics and watchful waiting for 48 to 72 hours
Red flags for mastoiditis or intracranial spread checked and absent
Complications such as perforation with otorrhea and persistent effusion with hearing loss kept in mind

easy: Toddler with a recent cold, fever, and ear tugging
Otoscopy shows a bulging, opacified tympanic membrane with loss of the light reflex
No pain with manipulation of the outer ear and no swelling behind the ear
medium: Infant who cannot localize pain and presents only with inconsolable crying and poor feeding
Older child with mild symptoms where watchful waiting is the right choice
Equivocal otoscopy requiring pneumatic otoscopy or tympanometry to confirm effusion
Concurrent upper respiratory infection with cough and nasal congestion
hard: Spontaneous perforation with otorrhea and sudden relief of pain
Symptoms persisting or worsening after 48 to 72 hours of appropriate antibiotics
Swelling or redness behind the ear with the auricle pushed forward suggesting mastoiditis
Severe headache, stiff neck, or lethargy suggesting meningitis or intracranial extension
Adult with ear fullness and hearing loss after a cold, with little fever
Immunocompromised child with rapidly worsening pain and high fever
